title: Self-Prompting Diffusion Transformer for Open-Vocabulary Scene Text Edit via In-Context Learning
claim: Prior methods condition on a separate glyph encoder and lose source style; ours prompts from the original image's own text.
layout: 2 stacked panels, left-to-right flow, dashed divider, ✗ vs ✓ outputs
description: The figure has two stacked panels separated by a dashed line. Panel (a), 'Previous OCR-based Text Editing', flows left to right. A stack of glyph images goes into a blue trapezoid labeled Glyph Encoder. A masked game-style image of three cartoon creatures with text goes into an orange VAE Encoder trapezoid. Both feed a purple Diffusion block. The output image shows 'Superpower' in a generic blue style, marked with a red X and a sad emoji. Panel (b), 'Self-prompting Text Editing', has no glyph encoder. The inputs are the rendered target text, a crop of the original red-flame 'Charmander' text, and the masked image. They are grouped by a bracket and go through the VAE Encoder and Diffusion. The output keeps the fiery style, with a green check and a smiley. Colors separate the modules, and the eye goes first to the creature images and the emojis.
caption: Comparison of previous OCR-based text edit and our proposed self-prompting text edit.
abstract: Scene text editing aims to modify text in a target region of an image while preserving surrounding background style and texture. Existing methods rely solely on image background information while neglecting the visual details of target regions, which discards stylistic features in the original text and essentially degrades the task to text rendering. Moreover, the conditions imposed by pre-trained glyph encoder limit the scope of editable text. To address these issues, this paper proposes a self-prompting scene text editing method that constructs style and glyph prompts directly from the original image, without introducing additional style or glyph encoders. We employ a two-stage training strategy: the diffusion transformer is first trained on large-scale self-supervised data and then refined using a small set of paired images. By leveraging the in-context learning capability of the Multi-Modal Diffusion Transformer (MM-DiT), it achieves open-vocabulary and style-consistent text editing. Experimental results on various languages demonstrate that our method achieves the state-of-the-art performance in both text accuracy and style consistency. Our project page: hongxiii.github.io/mstedit.
